title: Stochastic differential equations
Stochastic differential equations
text:
Reading the figure
In the first figure, the panel on the left shows twelve sample paths in orange, all started at \(x_0 = 2\) and simulated with Euler–Maruyama at \(\Delta t = 0.01\). Behind them, the blue line is the mean of a larger ensemble of 300 paths and the blue band is that ensemble’s mean plus and minus one standard deviation, as the legend under the panel says. The dashed black lines are the formulas for the Brownian and Ornstein–Uhlenbeck cases, mean plus and minus one standard deviation, so when the simulation is right the band and the dashed lines should agree up to sampling noise. The noisy spring has no dashed lines; its ensemble statistics would need a longer formula, and the band speaks for itself.
The panel on the right is a histogram of where the 300 paths are at the current moment, turned on its side so that it shares the vertical axis with the paths. The dashed curve is the Gaussian predicted by the formulas, or, for the spring, the Gaussian with the ensemble’s own mean and standard deviation. The three numbers above it are the ensemble mean, the ensemble standard deviation and the predicted standard deviation. The histogram is rescaled to fit its panel, so compare widths along the vertical axis, not bar lengths. Changing a slider or the model restarts the simulation from \(t = 0\).
The second figure runs the same random walk, \(dx = d\beta\) with \(D = 1\), twice with the time step you choose. On the left each step adds a standard normal number times \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\), on the right the same number times \(\Delta t\). The dashed lines in both panels are the same thing, the exact spread \(\sqrt{t}\) of the equation being solved, and the number under each panel is the measured standard deviation of 500 paths at \(t = 10\). The third panel collects that number for every available time step, blue for Euler–Maruyama and orange for naive Euler, against the exact value \(\sqrt{10}
\approx 3.16\) as a dashed line, with the current time step drawn larger.

title: Stochastic differential equations
text:
Things to try
Start with the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process at the default values. The mean decays from 2 towards 0 with time constant \(1/\theta\), and the band widens until it reaches a standard deviation of \(D/\sqrt{2\theta}\), which is 0.71 for the defaults. Once the mean has settled, the histogram on the right stops changing shape even though every individual path keeps moving. That is the stationary distribution, and it is what people mean when they say that an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process “has” a variance. Raise \(\theta\) and the band narrows and settles faster. Lower it and the process starts to look like Brownian motion for a while before the pull makes itself felt.
Switch to Brownian motion. Now nothing pulls \(x\) back, the mean stays at 2 and the band keeps growing as \(\sqrt t\), reaching a standard deviation of \(D\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2\) for \(D = 1\) at the end of the run. The histogram just keeps flattening. Set \(D\) to 2 and watch how many paths leave the plot: the standard deviation at \(t = 10\) is now 6.3, well beyond the axis.
Switch to the noisy spring. With \(\gamma = 1\) the mean oscillates a few times before it dies away, and the band is narrower than for the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process at the same \(D\), because the noise drives the velocity rather than the position and the spring filters it. Set the damping to 0.1 and the paths ring at the natural frequency for the whole run, still roughly in step with each other, while the mean decays only slowly and the band widens a little with every swing. Ten time units is too short to see where this ends up, but the trend is the point: the noise slowly knocks the paths out of phase with one another, so over a long enough run the mean fades away while every single path keeps oscillating. The ensemble mean is then a poor description of any member of the ensemble, which is worth remembering whenever a model is compared with trial-averaged data.
In the second figure, begin with \(\Delta t = 1\). The two path panels are indistinguishable, because \(\sqrt{1} = 1\), and the two dots in the third panel coincide on the dashed line. Go the other way first, to \(\Delta t = 2\) and then 5. With only five steps in the whole run the paths are crude in both panels, but the blue spread stays near 3.2 while the orange one climbs to 4.5 and then 7.1: a coarse step overstates the noise in the naive scheme just as a fine step understates it. Now reduce the step. The left panel stays the same apart from looking smoother, and its spread stays near 3.2 at every step: the blue dots sit on the line. The right panel shrinks. Its paths still spread as \(\sqrt t\), since it is a random walk like any other, only one with a weaker noise, and the spread at \(t = 10\) drops to 1.0 at \(\Delta t = 0.1\) and 0.32 at \(\Delta t = 0.01\). The orange dots fall away from the line as \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\). A numerical scheme is supposed to give an answer that stops depending on \(\Delta t\) once the step is small enough, and the naive one never does. In the limit of a vanishing step its noise would disappear altogether. This is the practical face of everything in the section on white noise. A random force that leaves a finite mark in a finite time must have an infinite amplitude in the limit, and the \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\) in the Euler–Maruyama scheme is the bookkeeping that makes that work on a computer. If a simulation of a noisy model gives results that change when you refine the time step, this is the first thing to check.
This page follows my 2022 coffee-meeting talk, which drew mostly on the lecture notes by Särkkä (2012), since published as a book (Särkkä and Solin 2019). Higham (2001) is the friendliest introduction to the numerical side and the source of the Euler–Maruyama figure in the talk. A disclaimer is in order: I once tried studying mathematics alongside biophysics and gave it up in favour of the physics part of my degree, so the mathematicians in the title may be angered by this page after all. If you are one of them, Särkkä and Solin (2019) has the proper version.

title: Stochastic differential equations
text:
Numerical details
Both figures use the Euler–Maruyama scheme exactly as written above, with standard normal numbers from the Box–Muller transform. The first figure integrates 300 paths with \(\Delta t = 0.01\) from \(x_0 = 2\) (and \(v_0 = 0\) for the spring) to \(T = 10\), draws 12 of them, and computes the mean and standard deviation across all 300 at every step; the spring uses \(\nu = 2\). The second figure integrates 500 paths of \(dx = d\beta\) with \(D = 1\) to \(T = 10\) at the chosen \(\Delta t\) and draws 15 of them; the convergence panel repeats the 500-path run for each of the nine available time steps with both schemes. The naive Euler scheme, with the noise increment multiplied by \(\Delta t\) instead of \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\), is used nowhere except in the right panel of that figure, where it is the point.

title: How I teach
text:
My first student was my brother. He was three, I was ten, and I had decided that he needed to understand how maths works. It went better than you would expect. He later skipped a year and sailed through school, so either the method worked or I made him stupidly smart, and I am not sure which. I learned something too: explaining a thing to someone who does not yet know it is the most fun you can have with an idea. I have not changed my mind since.
In the years after that I taught maths tutorials, first for physicists and later for biochemists, gave guest lectures in machine learning and in Theoretical Neuroscience, ran the computational neuroscience seminar with its sessions on how to read a paper, how to write one, and how to design a figure, and supervised Bachelor’s and Master’s theses. The interactive pages on this site come from the same impulse.1 This page is about what I have come to believe along the way. Believe is a strong word. I use it because it best captures the state of my knowledge: firmly held, and incomplete.

title: How I teach
text:
Learning happens with your hands
I am convinced that you learn something when you do it, not when you hear about it. For science that means, to me, doing the mathematics, even though I never formally studied it. You have to force yourself to play with a question, and playing means approaching it in every form it comes in: as an equation, as a picture, as a simulation, as a limiting case, as something you try to explain to someone else. Only then do you get to trust the answer, and even then only for now. The things I trust are the things I have taken apart myself, and I keep a list of the ones I have not.
In practice this shapes how I write exercises. I compose them, in the way a musician composes a piece, with a theme, a build-up, and a place where the student has to carry the melody alone. The task is rarely “derive the result” by itself. It is “derive the result, then implement it, then find the parameter range where it stops being true.” A simulation that produces the expected figure on the first try is a reason for concern, not celebration. Finding out why the integration step was too large, or why the noise term had the wrong scaling, is where the learning happens, and I try to leave room for that instead of handing out code that already works. A slider you can move while a model runs does the same job on a smaller scale, which is why these pages exist.

title: How I teach
section: Mathematics as a language, not a hurdle
text:
Mathematics as a language, not a hurdle
Students arrive in theoretical neuroscience from biology, physics, psychology, computer science and medicine, and their comfort with mathematics varies enormously. I do not think the answer is to water the mathematics down. The answer is to always say what a symbol means in words, to connect every equation to a picture, and to be explicit about which steps are routine and which are the actual idea. An eigenvector is a direction the matrix does not rotate. A Fourier transform asks how much of each frequency is in a signal. Once that is in place, the algebra is bookkeeping, and most people can do bookkeeping once they are told that is all it is. I say this with some authority. My father is a bookkeeper in the literal sense, a Steuerberater, and there was a time when I thought I would become one too.
In the same spirit, I try never to use an idea from a previous course without saying so. Being told “you have seen this before” when you have not is one of the fastest ways to lose someone.

title: How I teach
section: Confusion is where the good things come from
text:
Confusion is where the good things come from
Behaviour is always multidimensional. The people I teach will confuse me, and I will confuse them, and I have stopped treating that as a failure of either side. Some friction is exactly what you want: it is the sign that two ways of thinking have actually met. The trick is to keep it at a useful level, enough that something new can come out of it, not so much that someone gives up. A good deal of teaching, as I now understand it, is tuning that level.

title: How I teach
section: Diversity needs support, not just approval
text:
Diversity needs support, not just approval
I believe that diverse groups do better science, and the previous section is part of why. People who think differently ask different questions, notice different things in the same data, and catch each other’s blind spots. But wanting diversity is not the same as having it. A group that is open to everyone on paper and then runs on one unspoken set of habits, one way of speaking up in meetings, one idea of what a productive day looks like, will quietly lose the people it says it wants. Support has to be concrete: expectations written down, several ways to contribute and not just the loudest one, and the willingness to change how the group works when it is not working for someone.
I say this partly from the inside. I consider myself very neurodiverse. What I lack in diversity of outer appearance I make up for in inner chaos, and I have spent a good part of my career working out which structures let me do my best work and which ones get in the way. That makes me quicker to notice when a student is struggling with the format rather than the content, and more willing to change the format.

title: How I teach
section: Helping each other is the point
text:
Helping each other is the point
Science is not a solo sport, whatever the authorship conventions suggest. The groups I have enjoyed most, and that produced the best work, were the ones where asking for help was normal and giving it was expected. I try to make that the default in anything I run: in exercises, where I would rather students solve a sheet together and understand it than alone and not; in the seminar, where feedback on a draft or a practice talk is something everyone gives and everyone receives; and in supervision, where I want to be asked early rather than late.

title: How I teach
text:
My time with you
When I supervise someone, our meetings work like office hours. The time I have reserved is yours, and you can spend it on whatever is most useful to you right now: the derivation you are stuck on, the figure that will not come out right, the question of whether a PhD is the right next step, or something that has nothing to do with the project but is getting in the way of it. I will tell you at the start how much time I have that day, so that you can decide what to spend it on. And I will say so when I do not know the answer.
One small print: I am not a licensed doctor or psychotherapist, so I can only give oral referrals. They are drawn from vast experience, some of it my own, and they come with a warm recommendation to also ask someone with an actual licence.

title: How I teach
text:
Outreach is teaching too
Since 2019 I have helped organise the German Neuroscience Olympiad final in Frankfurt and run its computational tutorial, and for several years I was part of the team behind the Night of Science on the Riedberg campus. Teaching a sixteen-year-old why a neuron is a leaky bucket uses exactly the same muscles as teaching a master’s student about pattern formation, just with less notation. If anything, the younger audience is less forgiving of hand-waving, and I have brought more than one explanation back from the Olympiad into my university teaching because it worked better there.

title: The leaky integrate-and-fire neuron
The leaky integrate-and-fire neuron
The leaky integrate-and-fire neuron
text:
Reading the figure
The two panels on the left show 300 ms of the simulation. They work like an oscilloscope: the traces stay where they are and a grey cursor sweeps across, overwriting them, so your eye can rest on what has already been drawn; the Speed setting changes how fast the cursor moves. The upper panel is the input current, the lower one the membrane potential, blue while the input is noise-free and orange once you add noise. The red dashed line is the threshold, labelled in the panel. Each time the trace touches it you see a spike drawn up to +20 mV, then the voltage drops to the reset value and climbs again. The number in the corner is the firing rate, averaged since you last changed a setting.
The panel on the right is the f-I curve, the firing rate as a function of the input current. This is the standard way to characterise a neuron, and the page builds it up from your own experiments: every input strength you leave the neuron at for half a second adds a dot. Blue dots are noise-free measurements, orange dots were taken at the current noise level, and the dashed curve is the formula below. Changing the noise level clears the orange dots, because they no longer belong to the same curve. The open ring shows where the current setting sits.
The blue dashed line is the firing rate of the noise-free model worked out by hand rather than measured: the time the voltage needs to climb from reset to threshold under a constant current, plus the refractory period, is one interspike interval, and the rate is its inverse,
\[f = \frac{1}{t_{\text{ref}} + \tau_m \ln \dfrac{RI}{RI - (V_{\text{th}} - V_{\text{rest}})}} .\]
The formula makes two things obvious. Below the rheobase current \(I = (V_{\text{th}} - V_{\text{rest}})/R\), the voltage never reaches threshold and the rate is zero, so the curve has a hard corner. And at large currents the rate saturates at \(1/t_{\text{ref}}\), because the neuron cannot fire faster than once per refractory period.

title: The leaky integrate-and-fire neuron
text:
Things to try
Start with the noise off and raise the current slowly. Nothing happens until you cross 7.5 nA, and then the neuron starts firing at a rate that goes up quickly at first and then more slowly. Your dots should land on the dashed curve.
Now set the current to 6 nA, just below the rheobase, and turn on the noise. The voltage hovers below threshold and crosses it now and then, so the neuron fires at a low and irregular rate where the noise-free model is silent. Take a few measurements at different currents and compare the orange dots with the dashed line. Besides adding scatter, noise rounds off the corner of the f-I curve, and this smoothing is the main reason real neurons show no hard threshold in their rate.
Change the time constant. With a long \(\tau_m\) the voltage trace is smooth and the neuron is slow to respond, but the noise-free f-I curve shifts too, since a slower climb means a longer interval. With a short \(\tau_m\) and noise on, the trace becomes jagged and the firing increasingly random.
The model and the f-I formula are treated in Dayan and Abbott (2001, chapter 5) and at greater length in Gerstner et al. (2014), which also covers what noise does to the firing statistics. Brunel and van Rossum (2007) tell the story of Lapicque’s original paper.

title: The Hodgkin–Huxley neuron
The Hodgkin–Huxley neuron
The Hodgkin–Huxley neuron
text:
Reading the figure
The top panel is 25 milliseconds of membrane potential, enough for one or two spikes, drawn like an oscilloscope: the trace stays where it is and a grey cursor sweeps across, overwriting it, at a pace set by the Speed control. The number in its corner is the firing rate over the time since you last touched a slider. Below it are the three gating variables, each in its own panel on the same time axis: \(m\) in red, \(h\) in green and \(n\) in purple, with the legend under the panels. During a spike you can see the order of events: \(m\) shoots up first, then \(h\) drops and \(n\) rises together, and after the spike \(m\) falls at once while \(h\) and \(n\) take several milliseconds to recover. Simulated time runs much slower than real time, so that a spike that lasts one millisecond is visible; at the slow setting one sweep takes a few seconds.
The panel on the right is the f-I curve, firing rate against injected current. A point is added for each current you hold for at least 400 ms, blue when the conductances are at their standard values and orange when either has been changed, and the open circle marks the current setting. Reset clears the points.

title: The Hodgkin–Huxley neuron
text:
Things to try
Start at the default current of 10 µA/cm², where the neuron fires about 70 spikes per second, and lower it slowly. The rate falls a little, to about 55 spikes per second, and then at a current just above 6 the firing stops altogether. There is no setting at which the neuron fires slowly. This is the main difference from the integrate-and-fire neuron, whose rate rises smoothly from zero: the Hodgkin–Huxley neuron starts at a minimum rate or not at all, because the spike is an oscillation of the whole system, and an oscillation has a natural frequency. Neurons with this property are called type II, and the squid axon is the standard example.
Now raise the current. The rate climbs past 150 spikes per second at 120 µA/cm², but notice what happens to the spikes themselves: they get smaller as the current grows, and the trough between them gets shallower. By 140 the spike has shrunk to a ripple of about 15 mV, which is where the counter stops treating it as a spike, and at about 155 even the ripple is gone: the voltage sits at around \(-42\) mV with \(h\) stuck low and \(n\) stuck high. This is depolarisation block, and it is what the f-I curve on the right shows at its far end: the rate goes to zero at high current, which no integrate-and-fire model would predict.
Return the current to 10 and reduce the sodium conductance. At three quarters of its standard value the neuron is silent at this current but still fires if you raise \(I\) to 30; at half it does not fire at all, at any current in the range. This is what a sodium channel blocker like tetrodotoxin does. Now put sodium back and halve the potassium conductance instead. The neuron fires even with no injected current, at about 50 spikes per second, because the current that normally ends the spike and holds the membrane down is too weak. Raising the potassium conductance to one and a half times its value silences the neuron at any current in the range, which is the opposite effect.
The equations and parameters are those of Dayan and Abbott (2001, chapter 5), which follow Hodgkin and Huxley (1952) with the resting potential shifted to \(-65\) mV. The original paper is still readable and worth it; the Nobel lecture (Hodgkin 1963) tells the story of how the measurements were made.

title: Sampling and the discrete Fourier transform
Sampling and the discrete Fourier transform
Sampling and the discrete Fourier transform
text:
Reading the figure
The upper panel shows the signal. The thin grey curve is the true continuous \(y(x)\), which in a real experiment you would never get to see. The blue dots are the samples, the only thing the transform has access to. The orange curve is the signal rebuilt from the \(K\) strongest frequencies. When the orange curve lies on top of the grey one, the reconstruction has recovered the signal from its samples.
The lower panel is the amplitude spectrum. There is one stem for each grid frequency \(f_m = m/T\), with the height scaled so that a pure sine of amplitude \(a\) gives a stem of height \(a\). The red dashed line marks the Nyquist frequency, where the grid ends. The two green dashed lines mark where the true frequencies \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) ought to appear. If a true frequency lies above Nyquist, its green line is drawn at the frequency it gets aliased to, so you can see the stem land in the wrong place. Stems used in the reconstruction are drawn in orange, the rest in blue.
With the default settings everything is well behaved. Both frequencies sit on the grid, both are below Nyquist, the spectrum shows two clean stems of heights \(a_1\) and \(a_2\), and with \(K = 2\) the reconstruction is perfect.

title: Sampling and the discrete Fourier transform
text:
Things to try
Raise \(f_2\) slowly past the Nyquist frequency, which is 5 cycles per unit at the default sampling interval. Just below it the stem still sits where it should. Just above it, the green line and the stem jump to a lower frequency, and the orange reconstruction now contains a slow oscillation that was never in the signal. Look at the blue dots in the upper panel while you do this: they are consistent with that slower wave. Then make the sampling interval smaller. Nyquist moves up, the fast component is resolved again, and the problem goes away. That is the one reliable cure for aliasing: sample faster, or filter out the fast components before you sample.
Set \(f_1\) to 1 and change \(T\) from 4 to 4.5. The signal has not changed, but the grid has, and 1 cycle per unit no longer lies on it. The single stem turns into a cluster around the true frequency. With \(K = 2\) the reconstruction is now visibly wrong, and you need to raise \(K\) to get the signal back. The general lesson is that the width of a peak in a spectrum is set by the recording length, not by the signal, and that a sharp peak needs a recording that is long compared to the period.
Set both amplitudes to the same value and bring \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) close together. At some point the two stems merge into one, and no setting of \(K\) separates them. The frequency resolution is \(1/T\), so two frequencies closer than that cannot be distinguished, no matter how finely you sample.
This page is based on the Fourier exercises in Dayan and Abbott (2001). The transform here is computed by the direct sum, which is fine for a few hundred samples. For anything larger one uses the fast Fourier transform of Cooley and Tukey (1965), which gives the same numbers in a fraction of the time. Press et al. (2007) is a practical reference for both the algorithm and the pitfalls of sampling.

title: Two coupled neurons
Two coupled neurons
Two coupled neurons
text:
Reading the figure
The diagram on the left is the circuit. Neuron 1 is at the top and neuron 2 at the bottom, each drawn as a triangle if it makes excitatory synapses and as a circle if it makes inhibitory ones. The connection from 1 to 2 runs down the right side and the one from 2 to 1 up the left side. Each is red for excitatory and blue for inhibitory, ends in an arrowhead or a dot accordingly, and its thickness follows the strength slider. The two numbers under the diagram repeat the strengths.
The middle panel shows 200 milliseconds of both membrane potentials, neuron 1 in purple and neuron 2 in teal, with spikes drawn as vertical strokes to 20 mV. It works like an oscilloscope: the trace stays where it is and a grey cursor sweeps across, overwriting it, so your eye can rest on the part that has already been drawn. The dashed line is the threshold. The two numbers below are the firing rates, updated once per simulated second.
The panel on the right is the one to watch. Every time neuron 2 fires, a dot records when in neuron 1’s cycle it did so: 0 means at the same moment as neuron 1’s last spike, ½ means exactly halfway between two spikes of neuron 1, and values near 1 mean just before neuron 1’s next spike. If the two neurons fire in synchrony the dots sit at 0 or 1, which are the same thing. If they alternate, the dots sit at ½. The panel scrolls over the last five seconds, so you can see the phase settle from wherever the random start put it. At the slow setting a 200 ms sweep takes a second or two of real time; normal is about twice as fast and fast about eight times, which is useful for the phase panel, where it can take several simulated seconds for the dots to settle. Pause freezes everything.

title: Two coupled neurons
text:
Things to try
Start with the defaults: two inhibitory neurons, both strengths 0.2, and a synaptic time constant of 10 ms. After the random start, the dots in the phase panel drift to 0 or 1 within a second or two of simulated time, which is quicker to watch at the fast setting, and the traces fall on top of each other. Two neurons that do nothing but inhibit each other fire in perfect synchrony. The mechanism is in the traces: when one neuron fires, the other receives an inhibitory current that delays its next spike, and the delay is longer the closer to threshold the receiver was. The neuron that was ahead is held back more than the one that was behind, and the gap closes.
Make both neurons excitatory. Now the dots settle near ½, typically between 0.4 and 0.6: the neurons alternate. The argument runs the other way round. Excitation shortly after a neuron’s own spike, when it sits at the reset, does little, while excitation close to threshold triggers a spike immediately. The neuron that is behind is advanced more than the one ahead, and the gap opens until the two are as far apart as they can be. Van Vreeswijk, Abbott and Ermentrout (1994) made this precise, and their title says it all: when inhibition, not excitation, synchronises neural firing.
The synaptic time constant decides which of these two stories holds. Go back to two inhibitory neurons and set \(\tau_s\) to 3 ms. The dots move to ½: fast inhibition makes the neurons alternate, not synchronise. The reason is that the argument above assumed the inhibition is still present when the receiving neuron gets close to threshold, which requires the synapse to outlast a good part of the period. At 3 ms it has worn off before it can do its job. In the gamma models cited at the top, the inhibitory synapses have time constants around 10 ms, and the oscillation period is set by this number, which is why the rhythm sits where it does.
Try a mixed pair, one excitatory and one inhibitory, with equal strengths. After a second of drifting the dots settle at a fixed phase between the two extremes, and the two neurons fire at the same rate even though one is being excited and the other inhibited. This pair is the smallest version of the pyramidal-interneuron loop that generates gamma in the cortex. Make the excitatory synapse stronger than the inhibitory one and the lock breaks in an instructive way: the inhibitory neuron, which is being excited, fires two or three times per cycle of its partner, and the dots fall into several bands instead of one.
Then set one of the strengths to zero. With a one-way connection the receiver speeds up or slows down, depending on the sign, but at these strengths it does not lock to the sender: the dots form diagonal bands that drift through the panel, which is what two independent oscillators with slightly different periods look like. Locking needs the influence to go both ways, or a much stronger synapse. Finally, go back to the two inhibitory neurons and raise the drive to 40 mV. The rates roughly double, to about 130 spikes per second, and the pair still locks, but no longer in exact synchrony: the dots settle a little below 1, with one neuron leading the other by a few percent of the cycle. The period is now short compared with \(\tau_s\), and the lock is on its way to breaking. Shorten \(\tau_s\) at this drive and it does.
This page follows the exercise on synaptic coupling in Dayan and Abbott (2001, chapter 5), which in turn is based on van Vreeswijk et al. (1994).

title: Research Interests
text: I want to understand how a visual cortex that has never seen anything gets ready to see, and how the first days of visual experience turn that preparation into a reliable representation of the world. Everything below is a version of that question. I work on it with recurrent network models of cortical circuits and with chronically imaged populations of neurons in the developing ferret visual cortex, and I try to keep the models simple enough to take apart and the data close enough that the models have to answer to it.

title: Research Interests
text:
Structure before experience
The visual cortex is not a blank slate waiting for input. Already before eye opening, it shows spontaneous activity with a rich spatial organisation: patterns on the scale of millimetres, repeating with a characteristic wavelength, correlated across distant parts of the cortical sheet, and confined to a small number of dimensions. This organisation is generated to a large part by the cortex’s own recurrent circuitry; it persists when the retina and thalamus are silenced. Work from our group together with the Fitzpatrick lab, and from several other groups, has shown that the layout of these spontaneous patterns before eye opening predicts the layout of the orientation map that the same patch of cortex will have afterwards. The developing cortex, in other words, has a repertoire of patterns it readily produces before it has any visual reason to.
I want to know what this endogenous structure is for. One reading is that it is a scaffold: a set of preferred activity patterns that experience then selects among and sharpens. Another is that it is a constraint: whatever the cortex later learns has to be expressible in terms of patterns the network can already sustain. Both readings make predictions about what should happen at eye opening, and testing them is the thread running through my work.

title: Research Interests
text:
From variable to reliable
Models of cortical development have mostly been built to explain tuning and map layout: why a neuron prefers one orientation, and why neighbouring neurons prefer similar ones. They say much less about a property that is just as important for seeing, namely reliability. If the same stimulus is shown twice, does the cortex respond the same way twice?
At eye opening it does not. The response to a simple oriented grating varies strongly from trial to trial, and each response resembles one of the spontaneous patterns more than it resembles the response to the same grating a moment later. Over the following days this changes. Responses to the same stimulus become reproducible, responses to different stimuli become distinct, and an orientation map emerges that then stays stable. In Trägenap et al., Nature Neuroscience 2025 we followed this transition in individual ferrets, imaging the same region of cortex day after day through the week after eye opening, and asked what change in the circuit could account for it.
The explanation that fits the data is not that the cortex becomes quieter or that its noise goes down. It is that the visual input becomes aligned with the network’s own structure. The recurrent network amplifies some activity patterns and suppresses others, and reliability emerges once the feedforward drive for a stimulus comes to lie along the amplified patterns, so that the network’s response to a stimulus and its spontaneous activity begin to agree. A model in which this alignment is the only thing that changes reproduces the rise in reliability, the growing match between evoked and spontaneous patterns, and the time course over days. Models in which the input is merely strengthened, or the noise merely reduced, do not. (press release · free-to-read version)
I find this result appealing because it recasts the question of nature and nurture. The cortex arrives with a set of patterns it represents well. Experience does not have to build a representation from nothing; it has to bring the input into register with what is already there.

title: Research Interests
text:
Feedforward input meets recurrent circuits
This raises the next question: what is the feedforward input itself doing during that week? With the Fitzpatrick lab we looked at both sides of the junction, the thalamic input arriving in cortex and the cortical response it produces, across the same developmental window. In Lempel, Trägenap et al., Neuron 2025 we found that coherent cortical responses develop as two things change together. The feedforward inputs for different stimuli become more distinguishable from one another, and they become better aligned with the recurrent network they feed into. Neither change on its own accounts for the data. (press release · doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.08.014)
Part of what makes this hard to study is that two-photon imaging in the ferret does not reach the thalamic input layer, which lies too deep. So this work combines imaging of the superficial layers with electrophysiology and modelling to say something about the layer we cannot see.

title: Research Interests
section: Selective amplification across the cortical sheet
text:
Selective amplification across the cortical sheet
Underneath both results is a claim about the recurrent network: that it amplifies activity patterns with a particular spatial scale and suppresses others, acting as a pattern-selective filter. The classic account of how this could work is local excitation and wider inhibition, which pick out one wavelength. The Smith lab has tested this directly with patterned optogenetic stimulation: uniform light evokes modular activity at the network’s preferred wavelength, and patterns at other wavelengths are pulled towards it (Mulholland, Kaschube and Smith, 2024). The recurrent networks page in the Teaching section walks through the underlying mechanism in its simplest form.
With the Smith lab I am now asking which patterns the developing cortex amplifies on the scale of millimetres, how selective that amplification is, and which recurrent subnetworks can account for it. This is the work in Mulholland, Trägenap et al., bioRxiv 2026 (co-first authors; doi:10.64898/2026.03.31.715687). One thing we have learned along the way is that a perfectly uniform network of this kind would be too permissive, sustaining any pattern of the right wavelength equally well. It is the heterogeneity of real cortex, in connection strengths and in local anisotropies, that confines activity to a small set of patterns, and it is this set that the spontaneous activity reveals.

title: Research Interests
text:
A detour into skin
For several years, funded by the Center for Multiscale Modelling in Frankfurt, I also worked on models of pattern formation in the developing skin of cuttlefish. In the details this is a different subject, but the models belong to the same family: a field of interacting elements, local activation and longer-range inhibition, and a pattern with a characteristic wavelength that emerges from the interactions rather than from a template. Seeing the same mechanism at work in two systems that share no cells, no molecules and no evolutionary purpose was a useful reminder that the explanation lies in the structure of the interactions, not in the particular biology that implements them.

title: Research Interests
section: Looking ahead: across the animal tree
text:
Looking ahead: across the animal tree
Most of what we know about cortical development comes from a handful of species, and these species differ in instructive ways. Carnivores, primates and tree shrews have smooth orientation maps with a periodic layout and pinwheels; rodents have the same selectivity but arranged in a salt-and-pepper fashion, and their spontaneous activity shows none of the low-dimensional, map-like structure described above. Several hypotheses have been proposed for why, from cortical size to the density of thalamic afferents to the loss of an ancestral columnar organisation, and none has settled the matter. By comparing how the cortex is organised and how it develops across ferrets, cats, tree shrews and mice, I hope to separate the developmental principles that are shared from those that belong to one lineage. Where a species departs from the others, the departure points at the mechanism, and a theory that explains only one species is not yet a theory of the cortex.

title: Research Interests
section: Looking ahead: from biology to learning machines
text:
Looking ahead: from biology to learning machines
The developing cortex solves a problem that artificial systems also face: how to learn quickly from limited experience. The strategy we see in the brain is to start from a structured prior, generated by the network’s own dynamics, and to align incoming data with it rather than learn a representation from nothing. I am curious whether this strategy, made explicit, could make learning in artificial neural networks faster or more robust, and in the other direction, whether the tools built for understanding learning in deep networks can tell us something about what the cortex does in its first week of seeing.

title: Research Interests
text:
How I work
I sit between theory and experiment and I like it there. In practice this means dynamical recurrent network models of cortical circuits, analysis of large-scale two-photon and widefield calcium imaging data, and the comparison of the two: a model suggests what to measure, the measurement reshapes the model, and neither side gets to be right on its own. During my PhD I have done this in long-running collaborations with the labs of David Fitzpatrick (Max Planck Florida Institute for Neuroscience) and Gordon Smith (University of Minnesota). Much of what I have learned about doing science well has come from the friction between the way a theorist and an experimentalist look at the same figure.
A few habits follow from this. I prefer the simplest model that can be wrong, because a model I cannot break is a model I cannot learn from. Before fitting anything, I spend time on the question of what the model predicts that the data could contradict. And I try to make models playable: the parameter-exploration notebook linked below and the interactive pages in the Teaching section exist because changing a parameter and watching the pattern respond has taught me things that a derivation did not.

title: Eigenmodes of a recurrent network
Eigenmodes of a recurrent network
Eigenmodes of a recurrent network
text:
Reading the figure
The top left panel is the activity of all 40 neurons over time, one row per neuron, red for positive and blue for negative rates, scaled to the largest value seen so far. The colour scale is a square root, so that small activity late in the run stays visible. With no input, the activity is set at \(t = 0\) by the initial pattern you chose and then evolves on its own; with constant input it starts at zero and builds up. Rates below zero are not physical, but a linear model does not know that, and it is simplest to read the colours as deviations from a background rate.
The top right panel is the same activity after projecting it onto the eigenvectors of \(\mathbf M\). Each thin grey line is the amplitude of one mode on a logarithmic axis, so a pure exponential decay is a straight line whose slope is the decay rate. The slowest mode, the one with the largest eigenvalue, is orange, and the fastest, with the most negative eigenvalue, is blue. The dashed lines next to them are the solutions of the one-mode equation above, computed from the eigenvalue and the initial amplitude alone. They should sit on top of the simulated lines when the noise is off.
The bottom panel is the spectrum: all 40 eigenvalues sorted from largest to smallest, with the slow and fast modes coloured to match. The red dashed line at 1 is the stability limit. The spectral bound \(R\) moves the orange point up and down, and the rest of the spectrum scales with it.
The time axis is in units of \(\tau\), the time constant of a single neuron. The two time constants printed in the top right panel are in the same units.

title: Eigenmodes of a recurrent network
text:
Things to try
Start with a random initial pattern and no input at \(R = 0.9\). In the raster the activity fades within a few \(\tau\), but not to nothing: a faint pattern remains and dies away much more slowly. In the mode panel this is obvious. Every grey line drops steeply, the blue one steepest of all, while the orange line falls at a tenth of that slope: its time constant is \(1/(1 - 0.9) = 10\) times that of a single neuron. After a few \(\tau\) the orange mode is all that is left, and the surviving pattern in the raster is its eigenvector.
Now set the initial activity to the slowest mode alone. The raster shows a fixed pattern that just fades, and the mode panel is a single straight orange line, since nothing else was excited. Then pick the fastest mode. Its pattern alternates sign from neuron to neuron, so the recurrent input to each neuron opposes its own activity, and it is gone within a \(\tau\). The option with both modes shows the two decays together; after about two \(\tau\) the blue line has dropped below the grey floor and the raster has quietly switched from one pattern to the other.
Move \(R\). At \(R = 0.98\) the slowest time constant is \(50\,\tau\) and the orange line is nearly flat; the network has become a memory, holding its pattern long after the input is gone. At \(R = 0.5\) the slow mode lasts only twice as long as a neuron and the whole spectrum is compressed towards zero. At \(R = 0\) the matrix is zero, there is no recurrence, and all modes decay at the same rate.
Switch to constant input. Each mode now rises to its steady state \(h_i /
(1 - \lambda_i)\), and the dashed lines show the approach. The slow mode is amplified ten times at \(R = 0.9\), so the steady-state pattern of the network is dominated by its slowest eigenvector almost regardless of what the input looks like. This is the second thing recurrence does besides lengthening timescales: it filters the input, keeping the parts that match its slow modes and suppressing the rest. Click “New random network” to get a different matrix and a different slow pattern, and notice that the statements above do not depend on which one you got.
Finally add noise. The grey lines no longer decay but hover at a floor set by the noise, and the slow mode hovers highest on average, since it integrates the noise over the longest time. This is the network’s spontaneous activity, and its autocorrelation time is the slow mode’s time constant. A network can be made to look slow without any slow element in it, just by wiring fast elements into a loop that nearly closes. Measuring such timescales from recordings is harder than it looks, and much of what I know about it comes from the groups of Anna Levina in Tübingen and Tatiana Engel at Princeton. Fitting an exponential to an autocorrelation gives a biased answer for short recordings, and Zeraati, Engel and Levina (2022) show how to do it properly, by fitting the data with a mixture of exactly the kind of noisy modes shown here. In the same spirit, Shi et al. (2023) work out how spatially structured connections produce several timescales at once, one per spatial frequency, and Zeraati et al. (2023) find those multiple timescales in recordings from visual cortex, where the slow one lengthens with attention. The figure above is the toy version of all three: the spectrum of \(\mathbf M\) is the set of timescales, and \(R\) is the knob that attention would turn.
The exercise this page is based on is from the recurrent network chapter of Dayan and Abbott (2001, chapter 7). Rajan and Abbott (2006) describe what the spectrum of a random connection matrix looks like when excitatory and inhibitory neurons are distinguished, which the symmetric matrix here does not do.

Hebbian learning in the weight plane
Hebbian learning in the weight plane
text:
Reading the figure
The square on the left is the weight plane, \(w_1\) along the bottom and \(w_2\) up the side. The thick line is the trajectory from your starting point, which is marked by the open circle. It ends at the filled dot. Behind it, the faint lines are trajectories started from a grid of points, so you can see the overall flow of the rule at a glance. All of these are coloured by where they end up after 100 steps. For the bounded rule, blue means both weights saturated at 1, orange means \((0, 1)\) and green means \((1, 0)\). For Oja’s rule the end points are unit vectors instead, blue for \((1,1)/\sqrt2\), orange for \((-1,1)/\sqrt2\) and green for \((1,-1)/\sqrt2\). Grey means none of the above. Plain Hebbian learning is grey everywhere, since nothing ever stops.
The panel on the right shows the same trajectory as two curves against time, \(w_1\) in purple and \(w_2\) in teal. It is easier to see from this panel whether a weight has settled or is still moving.

title: Hebbian learning in the weight plane
text:
Things to try
Begin with the plain Hebbian rule and the default negative correlation. From any starting point the weights head off along a diagonal and leave the plot. Which diagonal depends on \(q\): the weights grow fastest along the eigenvector of \(Q\) with the largest eigenvalue, and that is \((1, 1)\) when the inputs are positively correlated and \((1, -1)\) when they are anticorrelated. Move \(q\) through zero and watch the flow swing from one diagonal to the other. At \(q = 0\) both eigenvalues are equal and every direction grows at the same rate, so the trajectories are straight rays from the origin.
Switch to the bounded rule. The runaway is gone, but something else has appeared: the plane is divided into regions, each draining into a different corner. A starting point that favours input 1 ends at \((1, 0)\), one that favours input 2 at \((0, 1)\), and with positive correlation most of the plane ends at \((1, 1)\). These regions are the basins of attraction of the three stable corners, and the bounds have turned a rule with no stable state into one that stores a decision about which input wins. Change \(q\) and watch the boundaries between the basins move.
Switch to Oja’s rule. Now the trajectories bend towards a circle of radius \(1/\sqrt{\alpha}\) and then slide along it to an eigenvector of \(Q\). The rule does two things at once: it normalises the weight vector and it picks out the direction of largest input variance, which is the first principal component of the inputs. This is the main reason Oja’s rule is famous. Raise \(\alpha\) and the circle shrinks. Set \(q\) to zero and the trajectories still reach the circle, but stop wherever they land on it, since no direction is preferred.
This page is based on the Hebbian learning exercise in Dayan and Abbott (2001, chapter 8). Miller and MacKay (1994) give a careful comparison of different ways of constraining Hebbian learning, including why subtractive and multiplicative normalisation lead to different outcomes, which is exactly the difference between the bounded rule and Oja’s rule above.

title: Teaching
text:
For the thinking behind these pages, see How I teach.
Most of my teaching material started out as Jupyter notebooks: exercises for the Theoretical Neuroscience lecture at Goethe University Frankfurt, and a webinar I gave for the German Neuroscience Olympiad in 2020. Notebooks are great for a course, but they are a hassle to open just to look at one plot. So I have moved the parts that benefit most from playing around onto these pages, where they run directly in the browser.
Each page has one small simulation and a handful of sliders. The simulation keeps running while you move a slider, so you can watch what a parameter does rather than read about it. The text is meant to make sense on its own, but it is not a replacement for the book. The exercises come from Dayan and Abbott’s Theoretical Neuroscience, and the format is borrowed from Dirk Brockmann’s Complexity Explorables.











The leaky integrate-and-fire neuron


The simplest model of a spiking neuron: a live membrane trace, a dose of noise, and an f-I curve that fills in as you explore.









Principal component analysis


Four measurements per flower, boiled down to two: what PCA does to the iris data, and why standardising the variables matters.









Sampling and the discrete Fourier transform


What happens to a signal when you only measure it at discrete points: the Nyquist frequency, aliasing, leakage, and rebuilding a signal from a few frequencies.









Recurrent networks: from kernel to pattern


How local excitation and wider inhibition single out one spatial frequency, and how a ring of neurons wired that way turns random input into stripes.









Hebbian learning in the weight plane


Why plain Hebbian learning runs away, and two ways to stop it: hard bounds and Oja’s rule, drawn as trajectories in the plane of two synaptic weights.









Stochastic differential equations


How to add noise to a differential equation without angering the mathematicians: an ensemble of sample paths, the Euler–Maruyama scheme, and the odd rule that noise scales…









Eigenmodes of a recurrent network


Why a linear network is easier to read in the basis of its eigenvectors: every mode decays or grows at its own rate, and the slowest one is the one that lasts.









Two coupled neurons


Two spiking neurons wired to each other through synapses: why mutual inhibition makes them fire together, mutual excitation makes them alternate, and the synaptic time…









The Hodgkin–Huxley neuron


The model that explains where the spike comes from: a live membrane trace with its three gating variables, sliders for the sodium and potassium conductances, and an f-I…

title: Principal component analysis
Principal component analysis
Principal component analysis
text:
Reading the figure
The large panel on the left is the scatter plot. Each dot is one flower, placed according to whatever you chose for the two axes. By default these are the first two principal components, so you are looking at the four-dimensional cloud from the angle that shows the most spread. Colour marks the species, blue for setosa, orange for versicolor and green for virginica. It is worth switching the colours off for a moment: the grey cloud is what PCA actually works with. The method never sees the species labels, and yet the three groups come out separated, because the differences between species are also the biggest source of variance in the data.
You can also put two of the original measurements on the axes. Then the plot is an ordinary scatter plot of those two columns, and on top of it the first two principal components are drawn as lines through the origin, PC 1 in red and PC 2 in purple. Each line is as long as two standard deviations of the data along it, so you see both where the component points and how much of the spread it captures. Note that the lines are projections of four-dimensional directions onto the two measurements you picked, so they need not look perpendicular.
The bars on the right show the share of the total variance that each component explains. With standardisation on, the first component accounts for roughly three quarters and the second for most of the rest, which is the justification for looking at only two of the four dimensions. Below the scatter plot is the table of loadings, the entries of each eigenvector. A loading says how much a given measurement contributes to a component. The first component has similar loadings on three of the four measurements with the same sign, so it is essentially “overall size of the flower”. The second is dominated by sepal width and separates flowers that are wide for their size from those that are narrow.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Things to try
Switch standardisation off and watch the loadings table. The first component is now almost entirely petal length, and the explained-variance share of PC 1 goes up, not because the structure got cleaner but because one variable with a large range now dominates. Then put petal length and sepal width on the two axes, with standardisation still off, and look at where the red line points.
Put the third and fourth components on the axes. There is almost nothing left to see, which is what a small eigenvalue means in practice: those directions are mostly measurement noise and natural variation within a species.
This page is based on the dimensionality-reduction exercise in Dayan and Abbott (2001). For how the same method is used on neural population recordings, where the “measurements” are the firing rates of many neurons, Cunningham and Yu (2014) is a good starting point. For a first encounter with PCA, the Stack Exchange answer that explains it over a family dinner is hard to beat.

text:
Pattern formation in a recurrent network
Now wrap 256 neurons around a ring, so that there are no edges to worry about, and connect each pair with a weight given by the kernel above. The firing rates \(r\) evolve according to
\[\tau \frac{dr}{dt} = -r + f\!\left(W r + h\right) .\]
Each neuron relaxes towards a function \(f\) of its total input, with time constant \(\tau\). The input has two parts: the recurrent input \(W r\) from the rest of the ring, and an external input \(h\) that is drawn at random once per neuron and then held fixed. On top of that you can add noise that is redrawn at every time step. The width sliders set the two Gaussians of the kernel, in units of neurons along the ring.

title: Recurrent networks: from kernel to pattern
Recurrent networks: from kernel to pattern
text:
Reading the figure
The upper panel shows the activity of every neuron as a bar, laid out by position on the ring, with the clock in units of \(\tau\) underneath. The lower panel shows the eigenvalues of \(W\), one grey dot for each spatial frequency, counted in whole waves around the ring. This is the same curve as the kernel spectrum in the first part of the page, just sampled at the frequencies that fit on the ring and scaled by the gain. The orange dot is the largest eigenvalue, and the red dashed line marks the value 1, the boundary between decay and growth.
With the default settings the gain is 1.2 and the orange dot sits above the line. After a moment the activity organises into a regular set of bumps, and if you count them you will find the number next to the orange dot. The random input is still there, which is why the bumps are not all the same height, but the spacing is set entirely by the kernel.

title: Recurrent networks: from kernel to pattern
text:
Things to try
Pull the gain below 1 and press Reset. The bumps fade and what is left is a noisy copy of the random input: the network is now a filter that smooths its input a little, nothing more. Push the gain back above 1 and the pattern grows back, from whatever small ripples in the input happen to match the favoured frequency. Near the threshold the growth is slow and you can watch it happen.
Make the inhibition wider. The orange dot moves left, to a lower frequency, and after a Reset the bumps are fewer and broader. Make excitation wider instead and the bumps get broader too, but the peak of the spectrum also gets flatter, so neighbouring frequencies compete and the pattern takes longer to settle.
Turn the noise up. The pattern survives surprisingly well, because the network amplifies only the component of the noise at its favourite frequency and ignores the rest. This is the sense in which a recurrent network with a Mexican hat kernel imposes its own structure on whatever it is given, and why the same mechanism has been proposed for so many different periodic patterns in the brain.
Now go back to the nonlinearity selector and switch to linear, with the gain still above 1. Press Reset and watch the axis labels of the activity panel: the stripes keep their shape but the numbers grow without bound, and the troughs go negative. Nothing in a linear network can stop a mode whose eigenvalue exceeds 1. Switch to the sigmoid and press Reset: the same network settles into bumps that can never exceed 1, however high you push the gain. At the default gain they are weak and noisy, because the sigmoid’s slope near its midpoint is modest. Push the gain up and the bumps sharpen into nearly binary blocks, with each neuron either fully on or fully off. Then try the rectified square with the default gain, and then with wider excitation: the narrower the peaks, the more the increasing slope feeds back on itself, and at some point the network runs away. Making inhibition stronger relative to excitation brings it back, which is the balance the supralinear network depends on.
This page is based on the pattern-formation exercise in Dayan and Abbott (2001, chapter 7). The ring network with a distance-dependent kernel is the setting of Amari’s (1977) analysis of neural fields, and the same architecture, with the ring standing for preferred orientation rather than position, is the ring model of orientation tuning of Ben-Yishai et al. (1995).
